How can I cope with the fear of losing my body or my life?
Why should I do my duty even when it involves hardship or danger?
Is there a part of me that is eternal and unchanging?
How do I come to terms with the death of loved ones?

questions: What really happens when someone dies?
Am I my body, or is there something deeper in me that doesn't die?
Do I actually kill someone if I fight in a war or defend myself?
Why do we fear death if the true Self cannot be killed?
How can I understand that the real me is not destroyed when the body ends?

2.20.summary: The Self (or soul) is never born and never dies; it is eternal, unchanging, and ancient, and is not destroyed even when the body is destroyed.
questions: What happens to me when I die?
How can I overcome my fear of death?
Is there a part of me that is eternal?
Why do I grieve for those who have passed away?
Does my true self ever die or cease to exist?

2.21.summary: This verse says that one who truly understands the Self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and undecaying cannot be the agent of killing or cause killing, because the Self is beyond birth and death.
questions: How can I come to terms with death if I believe the soul is eternal?
Does understanding the Self change how I see violence and harm?
What does it mean that the Self is never born and never dies?
If the Self is indestructible, why do we fear death?
How does knowing the Self affect my sense of responsibility for my actions?

2.22.summary: The verse compares the soul's transition from one body to another to a person discarding worn-out clothes and putting on new ones, emphasizing that the eternal self is not destroyed when the body dies.
questions: What happens to my soul when I die?
Will I ever see my loved ones again after death?
How can I overcome the fear of death?
Is there life after death?
Why do we fear losing our bodies if the soul is eternal?

2.23.summary: The Self (soul) is beyond all material elements—weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it—so it is completely indestructible.
themes: fearlessness in the face of death
questions: What happens to me when I die?
Can anything truly harm my real self?
Why should I not fear death?
Is there a part of me that is eternal and unchanging?
How can I understand that my true identity is beyond the body?

2.24.summary: The Self, or Atman, is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient, and cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried up, so understanding this, one should not grieve.
themes: inability of elements to affect the Self
questions: What part of me is truly eternal and cannot be destroyed?
Why should I not fear death if the Self is immortal?
How can I stop grieving over the loss of a loved one?
What is the real nature of my inner self?
How does understanding the eternal Self help me face physical changes and aging?

2.25.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Self is unmanifest, inconceivable, and unchanging, and that knowing this, Arjuna should not grieve for anyone.
questions: How can I stop grieving over the loss of a loved one?
What is the true nature of my inner self?
Why is it said that the soul cannot be understood by the mind?
If the Self never changes, why do we fear death?
How does knowing the Self is unmanifest help me deal with fear of death?

2.26.summary: Even if you hold the view that the Self is constantly being born and constantly dying, you still should not grieve, because such a cycle is inevitable.
themes: duty in the face of loss
questions: How can I stop grieving when someone I love dies?
Is it normal to feel sorrow when death feels like an endless cycle?
Why should I not grieve if life seems to be just a cycle of birth and death?
How do I accept that death is inevitable and still live fully?
Does believing in reincarnation mean I shouldn't mourn a loss?

2.27.summary: Since death is certain for the born and rebirth is certain for the dead, grieving over this unavoidable fact is pointless.
questions: Why do I grieve over death when it is inevitable?
How can I accept that everyone I love will eventually die?
What is the point of mourning if death is certain?
How does understanding the cycle of birth and death help me cope with loss?
Why does Krishna tell Arjuna not to grieve over something that cannot be avoided?

2.28.summary: All beings exist unmanifest before birth, become manifest in the middle, and return to the unmanifest after death, so there is no reason to grieve over this natural cycle.
questions: Why should I not grieve when someone dies?
What happens to us before birth and after death?
How can I accept the death of a loved one as natural?
Is there any point in mourning if death is inevitable?
How does understanding life's stages help me cope with loss?

2.29.summary: The Self is so profound that people respond to it in different ways—some see it as a wonder, some speak of it as a wonder, some hear of it as a wonder, and some, even after hearing, do not understand it at all.
questions: Why do some people seem to 'get' spiritual truths while others don't, even when they hear the same thing?
What does it mean to truly understand something versus just hearing about it?
How can I cultivate a deeper appreciation for the mystery of life?
Why is the true nature of the self described as a wonder?
What can I do if I hear spiritual teachings but they don't seem to sink in?

2.30.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Self dwelling in every body is indestructible, so he should not grieve for any living being.
questions: How can I stop grieving when someone I love dies?
What part of me is truly eternal and never dies?
Why does Krishna say I shouldn't grieve for any creature?
How does understanding the indestructible Self help me face loss?
Is it wrong to feel sadness when someone passes away?

2.31.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that even from the standpoint of his own worldly duty as a warrior, he should not hesitate, because no higher good exists for a Kshatriya than a battle fought for righteousness.
questions: Should I do what my role in life demands even when I feel conflicted about it?
How do I stop hesitating when I know what the right thing to do is?
Is there such a thing as a rightful fight, or should I always avoid conflict?
What does it mean to do my duty bravely in my own life and work?
How can I tell my duty from my fear when I'm facing something hard?

2.32.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that a warrior who is called to a righteous war without seeking it is fortunate, because such a battle is an open door to heaven.
questions: What should I do when a difficult but right opportunity comes to me without my asking for it?
How can I see a challenging situation as a chance for growth rather than a burden?
Is it wrong to feel happy about a duty that involves conflict?
How do I know if a responsibility that lands in my lap is truly meant for me?
What does it mean that doing my duty can lead to a higher reward?

2.33.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that refusing to fight this righteous war means abandoning his own duty and reputation, and thereby incurring sin.
questions: What happens if I avoid my responsibilities?
Is it wrong to walk away from a difficult situation that I know is right?
How important is my reputation when making tough choices?
Can I be blamed for not doing what I'm supposed to do?
What does it mean to abandon my duty?

2.34.summary: Krishna warns Arjuna that if he refuses to fight, people will spread endless tales of his disgrace, and for someone respected like him, that dishonor is worse than dying.
questions: Why does what other people say about me hurt so much?
How can I handle the fear of being publicly embarrassed or shamed?
Is it ever okay to avoid something just to protect my reputation?
How do I cope when people I respect start looking down on me?
Can the fear of losing respect push me to do something I don't want to do?

2.35.summary: Krishna warns Arjuna that if he withdraws from the battle out of fear, the great warriors who once respected him will think he fled in cowardice, and he will lose their esteem.
questions: What will people think of me if I back out now?
How do I handle the fear of being seen as a coward?
Is it worth risking my good name to avoid a difficult fight?
How can I maintain my self-respect when others might judge me?

2.36.summary: Krishna warns Arjuna that if he withdraws from the battle, his enemies will mock and insult him, which is a fate more painful than death.
questions: How do I handle the fear of being mocked or disrespected by others?

What should I do when my reputation is at stake?
How can I avoid letting others' insults control my actions?

2.37.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that whether he dies in battle and reaches heaven or wins and enjoys the earth, either outcome is good, so he should stand up and fight with determination.
themes: reward of heaven or earthly victory
questions: How can I move forward when I'm afraid of failing or even dying?
What if both outcomes of a difficult choice could be good?
How do I stop letting fear of loss paralyze me?
Is it okay to fight for what's right even if I might die?
How can I find the courage to do my duty when the stakes are high?

2.38.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna to fight with a balanced mind, treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat equally, and by doing so he will not incur sin.
questions: How can I stay calm when I'm facing both success and failure?
Why does treating wins and losses the same way matter?
How do I do my duty without being overwhelmed by pain or pleasure?
What does it mean to act without incurring sin?
How can I keep my mind steady when everything around me is changing?

2.39.summary: After explaining the path of knowledge (Sankhya), Krishna now introduces the path of Yoga (action with detachment), promising that it frees one from the bonds of action.

How can I act without being trapped by the results of my actions?
What does it mean to be free from the bonds of action?
Why does Krishna shift from knowledge to yoga here?
How can I apply this teaching to my daily work and responsibilities?

2.40.summary: Krishna begins describing the path of Yoga (action with detachment), saying that on this path no effort is ever wasted and no progress is lost, and that even a small amount of practice protects the seeker from great fear.
questions: If I can only meditate or practice for a few minutes a day, is it worth it?
Does my spiritual practice get lost if I mess up or stop for a while?
How can a little bit of spiritual practice protect me from fear?
What is the yoga that Krishna says has no loss or harm?
Why does Krishna say even a little of this knowledge saves one from great fear?

2.41.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that those who follow this path of spiritual understanding develop a single, focused conviction, while indecisive people are pulled in countless directions by endless, scattered thoughts.
questions: Why do I feel pulled in so many directions when trying to make an important decision?
How can I develop a single-minded focus on what really matters?
What makes my thoughts feel endless and overwhelming, and how do I calm them?
How do I stop second-guessing myself all the time?
What does it mean to be truly decisive, and why does it matter?

2.42.summary: After praising one-pointed determination, Krishna points out that those who are spiritually undiscerning get carried away by the flowery promises of Vedic rituals, believing that heavenly enjoyment is the only goal and remaining absorbed in desires for pleasure and power.

What if I achieve all the pleasures and powers I want—will that truly satisfy me?
How do I stop being fooled by beautiful words that only lead to more desire?
When I hear that there is 'nothing else' beyond material gains, how should I respond?

2.43.summary: Krishna describes people whose minds are full of worldly desires and who are drawn to rituals promising pleasure and power, aiming for heaven and new births, rather than seeking deeper spiritual understanding.
questions: Why do I keep chasing things that promise happiness but leave me empty?
Are religious rituals enough if my mind is still full of desires?
What is the point of aiming for heaven if I'm still caught in the cycle of rebirth?
How can I tell if my spiritual practice is just for show or for real growth?
Why do I get distracted by promises of pleasure and power instead of focusing on what truly matters?

2.44.summary: People who are deeply attached to pleasure and power and whose minds are swept away by ritualistic promises cannot develop a steady, one-pointed conviction needed for meditation and spiritual realization.
questions: Why can't I stay focused on my spiritual practice when I'm always chasing enjoyable experiences?
How do constant desires for comfort and success keep me from deeper concentration?
Why do I feel spiritually stuck even though I follow religious routines?
What is missing in my life that prevents me from having unwavering faith and focus?
How can I tell if my mind is too pulled by worldly promises to meditate deeply?

2.45.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna to go beyond the Vedas' focus on the three gunas and ritual rewards, and instead free himself from dualities like pleasure and pain, remain centered in sattva, let go of acquiring and keeping things, and become established in the Self.
questions: How do I stop being controlled by pleasant and unpleasant experiences?
What does it mean to go beyond the rewards promised by religious rituals?
How can I find steady inner balance in daily life?
How do I let go of constantly trying to get and keep things?
What does it mean to be established in the Self?

How do I do my work without getting attached to how it turns out?
What does it really mean to be 'even-minded' in daily life?
How can I keep my balance when things go well or badly?

How can I tell if I'm growing in inner stability?

What does it mean to be truly wise and stable in daily life?

How can I stop myself from becoming attached to things I keep thinking about?

What happens if I keep chasing after things I want?

How do I find peace when I'm constantly pulled by likes and dislikes?
Can I interact with the world and still stay calm inside?

How can I make my understanding of life stable and unshakable?
What is the connection between controlling my senses and being peaceful?
How does peace help me gain deeper knowledge?

Why is it so hard to stay focused on what matters?
What's the link between a restless mind and lack of peace?
How do I gain deeper wisdom about life?

What happens to my ability to think clearly when I chase after pleasures?
Why does my wisdom seem to disappear when my senses run wild?
How can I stay steady and focused when my senses keep wandering?

questions: How can I keep my senses from pulling me away from what I know is right?
What does it mean to have steady knowledge or wisdom?
Why is controlling my senses so important for spiritual growth?
How do I stop being distracted by sights, sounds, and other things I crave?
Is it possible to live in the world without being controlled by my senses?

What does it mean to be truly awake in life?

How do I balance worldly life and inner awareness?

questions: How can I stay calm when I keep wanting more and more things?

What does it mean to be at peace even when things are constantly changing around me?
How can I stop letting my cravings control my happiness?

questions: How can I find peace when I always want more?
What does it mean to live without a sense of 'me and mine'?
How do I stop feeling possessive about people and things?
Is it possible to be free from pride and still function in the world?
Why does letting go of desires bring peace?

questions: What is the ultimate goal of life according to the Gita?

Does spiritual realization only matter at the end of life?
What does it mean to be established in Brahman?
Can I attain oneness with the divine even if I start late?

How do I know which path will truly help me grow?
What should I do when my spiritual beliefs conflict with my daily responsibilities?

Does renouncing the world automatically make me perfect?
Why can't I just avoid all actions to find peace?
What's the difference between not acting and truly renouncing?

What makes me act even when I try to be still?
Why do I feel forced to keep busy all the time?
Does renouncing actions really free me from acting?

questions: How do I know if I'm just pretending to be disciplined or spiritual?
Why can't I stop thinking about things I've given up on the outside?
Is it enough to control my actions but not my thoughts?
What does it mean to be a hypocrite in my spiritual life?
How can I tell the difference between real renunciation and just going through the motions?

3.7.summary: Instead of merely restraining the senses while still dwelling on sense objects mentally, one should control the senses with the mind and engage in selfless action without attachment, thereby excelling.
questions: How can I stop just talking about change and actually do something?
What does it mean to act without being attached to the outcome?
How do I control my senses instead of just suppressing them?
Why is it better to act than to sit idle?
How can I serve others without expecting anything in return?

What does it mean that action is superior to inaction?

questions: How can I work without feeling trapped by my job?
What does it mean to do something for God instead of for myself?
How do I stop being attached to the results of my actions?
Can everyday tasks become a form of worship?
Why do good deeds sometimes still make me feel stuck?

3.10.summary: The Creator, at the beginning of creation, established the principle of sacrifice (yajna) as a means for humanity to prosper and fulfill their desires through mutual support between humans and the gods.
questions: What is the purpose of sacrifice in life?
How can I prosper and fulfill my desires?
What is the relationship between humans and the divine?
Why is it important to give back to the world?

3.11.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that when humans give to the divine powers through sacrifice, those powers give back to humans, and by this mutual giving, both reach the highest good.
questions: Why should I give anything at all?
Does giving guarantee I'll get something back?
How does taking without giving harm me?
What does it mean to 'nourish the gods' today?
How can giving and receiving lead to the highest good?

3.12.summary: Building on the idea that gods and humans nourish each other, this verse warns that enjoying the gifts and pleasures the gods provide without first giving back to them in sacrifice makes one a thief.
questions: How can I enjoy my blessings without feeling guilty?
Why should I give back when I've worked hard for what I have?
What does it mean to be a thief in a spiritual sense?
How do I balance enjoying life and being generous?
What is the right way to show gratitude for what I receive?

3.13.summary: Those who eat food that has first been offered in sacrifice are freed from sin, while those who prepare food only for themselves eat sin.
questions: Why should I share what I have instead of keeping it all for myself?
How can I practice gratitude before enjoying what I receive?
Does it really matter if I only look out for myself?
What does it mean to eat 'sin'?
How can I make my daily meals more meaningful and less selfish?

3.14.summary: This verse explains a cyclical chain of interdependence: living beings are sustained by food, food is produced by rain, rain comes from sacrifice (proper ritual action), and sacrifice originates from action.
questions: Where does our food really come from?
How are all things in life connected?
What is the purpose of performing sacrifices?
How does action lead to the cycle of life?
How can I understand the chain of cause and effect in the world?

3.15.summary: This verse continues the description of the cosmic cycle by tracing action back to the Vedas, the Vedas to the imperishable source, and concludes that the all-pervading reality is forever established in sacrifice.
questions: What is the ultimate source of everything I do?
How is my daily work connected to something eternal?
Why is sacrifice considered the basis of all action?
What does it mean that the Vedas come from the Imperishable?
How can I see my actions as part of a larger cycle?

3.16.summary: This verse warns that anyone who does not participate in the natural cycle of selfless action and sacrifice, but instead lives only for sensory pleasure, wastes their life and incurs sin.
questions: What happens if I ignore my responsibilities and just chase pleasure?
Why is it important to do my part in the bigger picture?
How can I avoid wasting my life on temporary pleasures?
Is it wrong to enjoy sensory pleasures?
What does it mean to live a sinful life according to the Gita?

3.17.summary: This verse says that a person who delights, is satisfied, and content solely in the Self has no duties or obligations to perform, because they are already fulfilled and need not act for personal gain.
questions: If I'm completely happy with who I am, do I still need to do my job or other responsibilities?
How can I find satisfaction within myself instead of always chasing external goals?
Does being spiritually fulfilled mean I can ignore what others expect of me?
What does it mean to rejoice only in the Self?
Is there a point where I no longer have to worry about doing the right thing?

3.18.summary: This verse says that a person who completely delights in the Self and is satisfied within has no obligation either to act or to refrain from action, and depends on no external thing or being to fulfill any purpose.
questions: Do I still have to do my duties if I feel completely content inside?
Why do I feel I need things or people to be happy?
What does it mean to have no interest in what is done or not done?
How can I become so satisfied that I no longer depend on anything outside?
If I am self-satisfied, does that mean I can stop doing anything at all?

3.19.summary: Since the enlightened have no personal stake in action or inaction, you should still carry out your obligatory duties without attachment, because doing so leads to the highest spiritual goal.
questions: How can I do my job without being attached to the results?
What does it mean to do my duty without selfishness?
Can I reach spiritual growth while still being active in the world?
How do I keep doing my responsibilities when I feel no personal gain from them?
What is the highest goal I can attain by working selflessly?

3.20.summary: King Janaka and others reached spiritual perfection by doing their duties, so you too should act, not only for your own liberation but also to set a good example and keep society on the right path.
questions: How can I grow spiritually while still working and fulfilling my daily responsibilities?
What can I learn from people who balanced worldly duties with inner peace?
How do my actions influence others, even when I don't realize it?
What should I do if I'm in a position where others look up to me?
How can I help keep society on the right track through my own work?

3.21.summary: Whatever a great or respected person does, others imitate, and whatever they establish as a standard, the world follows.
questions: How can I be a good role model for my children or coworkers?
What kind of example am I setting for others by my actions?
Why should I care about how my behavior influences others?
How do leaders set the tone for their teams or communities?
Should I adjust my actions knowing that others might follow them?

3.22.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that although he has no personal duties or unfulfilled goals in all the worlds, he still engages in action, setting an example for others to follow.
questions: Why should I work if I don't need anything?
How can I lead by example in my community?
What does it mean to act without personal motive?
How do my actions influence others?
Can I be active without being attached to results?

3.23.summary: Krishna says that if he ever stopped engaging in action, people would follow his example in every way, so he must continue to act to set the right example.
questions: Why should I keep working hard when I feel like I've already made it?
How can I be a good role model for others when I'd rather take it easy?
Do the people around me really pay attention to what I do?
If I stop doing my duties, what effect will that have on my family or team?
What responsibility do I have to others as a leader or parent?

3.24.summary: Krishna warns that if he stopped working, the whole world order would collapse into ruin and confusion, so even he must remain active.
themes: the necessity of action for world order
questions: What happens if I stop doing my duties?
Do leaders have a responsibility to keep working even if they don't need to?
Can my inaction harm others?
How does my work affect the world around me?

3.25.summary: An enlightened person should act without selfish attachment, just as ignorant people act out of attachment, but with the aim of guiding others and preventing them from going astray.
questions: How can I help others without being attached to the outcome?
What does it mean to act for the welfare of the world?
How do I set a good example for others who are less aware?
Should I change my behavior to guide those who are attached to results?
How can I stay detached while still being fully engaged in my work?

3.26.summary: A wise person should not disrupt the beliefs of those who are attached to action, but should instead diligently perform their own duties and encourage others to do the same, without attachment.
questions: How can I help someone who is stuck in their ways without upsetting them?
Should I try to change others' beliefs if I think they are wrong?
How can I be a good role model for others while staying true to my own path?
What is the best way to guide someone who is not ready for deeper truths?
How do I balance my own spiritual growth with helping others grow?

3.27.summary: Actions are actually carried out by the qualities of nature (the gunas), but one who is deluded by ego thinks 'I am the doer,' which leads to bondage.
questions: Why do I take everything personally and think I'm the one doing everything?
How can I stop feeling like I'm the sole author of my actions?
What does it mean that nature does everything and not me?
How does egoism make me suffer when I act?
If I'm not the doer, who is?

3.28.summary: One who truly understands that the senses and their objects are all made of the gunas of Nature acts without attachment, knowing that it is the senses interacting with sense-objects, not the Self who acts.
questions: How can I stop feeling like I'm the one doing everything?
What does it mean to act without attachment?
How do I detach from my senses when they pull me toward things?
What is the difference between the Self and the mind-body?
How can understanding the gunas help me be less reactive?

3.29.summary: Those who are deluded by the three gunas (qualities of nature) become attached to the actions produced by those gunas, but a person of true knowledge should not unsettle or disturb such ignorant people who do not know this truth.
questions: Why do people get so attached to what they do, even when it causes them suffering?
Should I try to correct someone who is clearly wrong, or is it better to leave them alone?
How can I help others without making them feel inferior or confused?
What should I do when I see people acting out of ignorance and attachment?
Is it my responsibility to change the way others think and act?

3.30.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna to offer all his actions to the Divine, keep his mind fixed on the Self, let go of expectations and egoism, and, free from inner agitation, simply do his duty and fight.
questions: How can I do my work without obsessing over whether it will succeed?
How do I stop making everything about me and my ego?
What does it mean to dedicate my actions to God in daily life?
How can I stay calm and focused when I'm anxious about a big decision?
How do I do what I have to do even when I dread it?

3.31.summary: Those who faithfully practice the teaching of offering all actions to the Divine, without doubt or fault-finding, are also freed from the bondage of their actions.
questions: What does it mean to follow the teaching of selfless action with faith?
How can I practice offering all my actions to God and still live a normal life?
Why is it important not to find faults with spiritual teachings?
What happens if I practice selfless service but have doubts?
How does faithfully following the Gita's teachings free me from the consequences of my actions?

3.32.summary: Krishna contrasts the faithful who follow his teaching and are freed from karma with those who find fault with it and refuse to practice, calling the latter deluded and devoid of discernment, and thus headed for ruin.
questions: Why do I sometimes criticize advice that could help me instead of just trying it?
What happens if I keep ignoring teachings that everyone says are good for me?
How can I tell if I'm being genuinely discerning or just stubbornly fault-finding?
Does refusing to practice what I know is right really lead to a bad outcome?
What does it mean to be 'deprived of knowledge' in everyday life?

3.33.summary: Even a wise person naturally acts according to their own inborn nature, and everyone follows their nature, so mere external restraint or suppression cannot change how people behave.
themes: acting in line with one's disposition
questions: Why can't I just force myself to be someone I'm not?
Does self-discipline mean fighting my own nature?
If everyone follows their nature, does self-control even matter?
Why do I keep falling back into old patterns no matter how hard I try?
How can I work with my natural tendencies instead of against them?

3.34.summary: The senses naturally feel attraction or aversion toward the objects they encounter, but these feelings are enemies that one should not let control them.
questions: Why do I keep getting pulled toward things I know aren't good for me?
How can I stop letting my likes and dislikes control my decisions?
Is it possible to live without being ruled by cravings and aversions?
Why do my senses feel like they're fighting against me?
How do I stay steady when something I want or hate shows up?

3.35.summary: It is better to perform your own duty imperfectly than to perform someone else's duty well, because following your own path, even if it leads to death, is preferable to the fear and danger of imitating another's role.
questions: Should I stay in my current job even if I'm not great at it, rather than switching to something I might be better at?
How do I know what my true duty is?
Is it wrong to try to be like someone else if they are more successful?
Why is it better to fail at my own path than to succeed at someone else's?

3.36.summary: Arjuna asks Krishna what force makes a person commit sin even against their own will, as if compelled by something stronger than themselves.
questions: Why do I do things I know are wrong, even when I don't want to?
What makes me act against my own better judgment?
Is there something inside me that forces me to mess up?
Why can't I just stop doing the things I regret?
What is it that pushes me to hurt others or myself?

3.37.summary: Krishna answers Arjuna's question about what forces people to sin by identifying selfish desire and anger, born from the restless rajas quality of nature, as the all-consuming enemy within.
questions: Why do I keep doing things I know are wrong, even when I don't want to?
What is the real reason behind my anger and cravings?
How can I recognize the enemy inside my own mind?
Is desire always bad, or only when it becomes selfish and out of control?
How do I stop being controlled by my wants and frustrations?

3.38.summary: Continuing the description of desire as the enemy, this verse compares how desire and anger conceal our inner wisdom to the way smoke hides fire, dirt covers a mirror, or a womb encloses a fetus—each image showing something pure and essential being obscured.
questions: Why does desire hide the truth even when I know better?
Is anger something external or part of me that clouds my judgment?
How can I tell what my real wisdom is when my cravings keep covering it up?
Am I born with this inner clarity already buried, and if so, how do I uncover it?

3.39.summary: This verse states that desire—an insatiable, ever-present enemy of wisdom—covers the knowledge of even the wise.
themes: desire as an obstacle to wisdom
inner conflict between desire and knowledge
questions: Why do I keep wanting more even when I know it won't make me happy?
How can I recognize when my desires are clouding my judgment?
What can I do to keep my cravings from overpowering what I know is right?
Why is desire considered an enemy even for wise people?
How do I deal with the feeling that I never have enough?

3.40.summary: This verse explains that desire, the enemy of wisdom, operates through the senses, mind, and intellect, and uses them to delude the embodied soul and veil its knowledge.
questions: Why do my own senses, mind, and intellect sometimes work against my better judgment?
How does desire use my own faculties to cloud my understanding?
What is really going on inside me when I feel pulled away from what I know is right?
How can I recognize when my mind is being used to delude me?
If desire is inside my senses and mind, how can I ever get free from it?

3.41.summary: After describing how desire and anger delude a person by clouding their knowledge, Krishna instructs Arjuna to first bring the senses under control and then completely overcome this sinful desire, which destroys wisdom and self-realization.
themes: spiritual growth through mastery of the mind
questions: How can I stop letting my desires control me?
Why do my cravings make it hard to think clearly?
What should I do first to gain control over my impulses?
How can I overcome anger and greed that ruin my peace of mind?
Is it possible to live in the world without being ruled by my senses?

3.42.summary: This verse describes a hierarchy of human faculties—body, senses, mind, intellect—and points to the Self (or God) as higher than all of them, setting the stage for using that higher awareness to overcome desire.
themes: hierarchy of body, senses, mind, intellect, and Self
the Self as superior to the intellect
self-mastery through knowledge of the Self
desire as an enemy to be conquered
questions: What is the difference between my mind, my intellect, and my true self?
How can I use my higher self to control my desires?
Why does the Gita say the Self is higher than the intellect?
How do I stop being ruled by my senses and mind?
What does it mean to 'restrain the self by the Self'?

3.43.summary: After explaining that the Self is higher than the intellect, Krishna tells Arjuna to use the mind to control the senses and, by realizing the Self, to destroy the enemy of desire, which is hard to overcome.
questions: How do I stop being controlled by my cravings?
What is the best way to deal with my inner demons?
How can I use my mind to overcome bad habits?
Why is desire considered an enemy?
How does knowing my true self help me defeat desire?

4.1.summary: Krishna begins a new teaching by revealing that this eternal yoga was originally given to Vivasvan (the sun god), passed down through Manu and Ikshvaku, but has been lost over time.
questions: What is the origin of the yoga that Krishna is teaching?
Who were the first people to receive this teaching?
Why does Krishna say this ancient yoga was lost?
How does this teaching reach us today if it was lost?
What does it mean that the yoga is imperishable?

4.2.summary: Krishna explains that the ancient yoga He originally taught was passed down in succession through royal sages, but over a long period of time it became lost.
questions: Why do ancient teachings sometimes get lost over time?
How can I reconnect with wisdom that seems forgotten?
What does it mean that this yoga was passed down through kings?
Why does Krishna call Arjuna the destroyer of foes here?

4.3.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that he is now teaching him the same ancient yoga that was lost over time, because Arjuna is his devotee and friend, and this teaching is a profound secret.
questions: Why is spiritual knowledge often kept secret?
What qualities make someone ready to receive deep teachings?
How can I find a teacher I can trust?
Is it important to have a personal connection with a spiritual teacher?
How do ancient teachings remain relevant today?

4.4.summary: Arjuna questions how Krishna could have taught the ancient yoga to Vivasvan (the Sun god) in the distant past, since Krishna was born much later than Vivasvan.
questions: How can I trust a teacher whose story doesn't add up?
What does it mean to have a teaching that is older than the teacher?
If someone claims to have taught something in a past life, how can I understand that?
Why do spiritual teachers sometimes make claims that seem impossible?
How do I reconcile modern ideas of time with ancient stories of gods and sages?

4.5.summary: Krishna answers Arjuna's doubt about how he could have taught the sun god in the distant past by explaining that both he and Arjuna have had many past lives, but while Krishna remembers them all, Arjuna does not.
themes: eternal relationship between God and soul
questions: Do we really have past lives, and why can't I remember mine?
How can God know everything about me while I don't even know my own past?
Does God remember all my past actions and lives?
How can I trust that God has always been with me even when I feel alone?
What does it mean that God remembers our past lives but we forget them?

4.6.summary: Krishna explains that although he is unborn, imperishable, and the Lord of all beings, he voluntarily takes birth by his own power and control over his nature.
questions: If God is unborn and unchanging, why does He take birth as a human?
How can someone be born without being forced by karma or nature?
What does it mean that God governs His own nature and is born by His own Maya?
How does this verse help me understand the difference between God's birth and my own birth?
Why would the Lord of all beings choose to be born into this world?

4.7.summary: Krishna explains that whenever goodness and righteousness decline and evil rises in the world, he takes on a visible form and appears among people.
questions: Why does God allow bad things to happen in the world?
Is there a higher power that steps in when things get really bad?
What does it mean when society seems to be falling apart morally?
How can I trust that good will ultimately prevail?
Does God really come to earth in human form?

4.8.summary: Krishna explains the purpose of his repeated incarnations: to protect the good, destroy evil, and restore righteousness in every age.
questions: Why does God take birth again and again?
How does God protect good people in the world?
What is God's role in destroying evil?
How does God restore righteousness when it declines?
Does God appear in every age to help humanity?

4.9.summary: Knowing the true nature of Krishna's divine birth and actions frees a person from the cycle of rebirth and leads them to attain him after death.
questions: What happens after we die?
How can I break free from the cycle of reincarnation?
What does it mean to truly know God?
Can understanding Krishna's divine nature change my destiny?
How do I attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death?

4.10.summary: Many people before you, who let go of attachment, fear, and anger, took refuge in the Divine and were purified by the fire of knowledge, have attained the same divine state.
questions: How can I let go of my attachment to outcomes I can't control?
What does it mean to take refuge in something greater than myself?
How do I deal with fear and anger that keep coming up?
Is it possible to purify my mind through understanding?
What does it take to reach a state of lasting peace?

4.11.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that He responds to each person in whatever way they approach Him, and that people follow His path in many different ways.
questions: Does God answer everyone in the same way?
Are there multiple paths to the divine?
How does God respond to my prayers if I approach Him with different intentions?
Can people from different religions all be following the same ultimate path?
What does it mean that God meets me according to how I approach Him?

4.12.summary: People who are eager for quick results from their actions worship the gods, because in the human world success obtained through action comes quickly.
questions: Why do people chase after quick results instead of deeper meaning?
Is it wrong to pray for success in my career or finances?
How can I tell if I'm only doing things for the reward?
What does it mean that success comes quickly through action?
Should I stop asking for things and just do my duty?

4.13.summary: Krishna says that the four social classes were created by Him based on people's qualities and actions, yet even though He is the author of this system, He remains a non-doer and unchanging, not personally attached to the act.
themes: four castes by qualities and actions
questions: Does God really make different social classes?
If God created the caste system, why is it so unfair?
How can God do something and still not be the doer?
What does it mean that God is unchanging?
What determines someone's caste according to the Gita?

4.14.summary: Krishna says that although he acts, he is not tainted by action because he has no desire for the results, and that anyone who understands this also becomes free from the bondage of their actions.
questions: How can I work hard without being tied down by worrying about what I'll get out of it?
What does it mean to act without desiring the fruits of my actions?
How can I be free from the consequences of my actions?
If I understand God's nature, how does that change the way I act?
Why do actions not affect someone who has no longing for results?

4.15.summary: Having understood that actions do not bind the one who knows the Self, even ancient seekers of liberation performed their duties; therefore, you too should act as the ancients did.
themes: following the example of the wise
questions: How can I fulfill my responsibilities without feeling trapped by them?
What does it mean to act like the ancient sages in my everyday life?
If I understand that actions don't bind me, does that mean I can do whatever I want?
How do I balance spiritual growth with my worldly duties?
Can I achieve freedom while still being active in the world?

4.16.summary: Krishna acknowledges that even wise people are confused about what truly counts as action versus inaction, and promises to explain this knowledge that frees one from the cycle of birth and death.
questions: What does it really mean to act or not act?
Why is it so hard to tell if I'm doing the right thing?
How can understanding action free me from the cycle of rebirth?
If even wise people are confused, how can I know what to do?
What is the difference between doing nothing and truly being inactive?

4.17.summary: Krishna explains that to truly understand action, we must also understand what is forbidden and what is inaction, because the real nature of action is very difficult to grasp.
themes: the complexity of action and inaction
the need for knowledge of what is prescribed and prohibited
questions: What exactly counts as doing something versus not doing anything?
How can I tell if I'm doing the right thing or something I shouldn't?
Why is it so hard to understand the consequences of my actions?
What does it mean to be truly inactive while still doing things?
How can I know if I'm really responsible for what happens?

4.18.summary: One who sees inaction within action and action within inaction is truly wise and is a yogi who acts rightly, because their understanding of action and inaction is reversed from the ordinary view.
questions: How can I be active in the world yet inwardly detached?
What does it mean to act without really acting?
How do I know if I'm truly doing the right thing?
How can I work hard without feeling bound by my actions?
What makes someone wise in the way they act?

4.19.summary: This verse describes the truly wise person as one whose actions and thoughts are free from desire and selfish motive, and whose actions have been burned away by the fire of knowledge.
questions: How can I act without being driven by selfish desires?
What does it mean to burn up my actions with knowledge?
Who is considered truly wise in spiritual life?
How do I stop my thoughts from being controlled by wants?
Can my past actions be neutralized by wisdom?

4.20.summary: One who has let go of attachment to the results of actions, remains ever content, and depends on nothing, is not truly acting even while engaged in activity.
questions: How can I work hard without being attached to the outcome?
What does it mean to be content and depend on nothing?
If I give up caring about results, will I still be motivated?
How can I act without feeling like I am the doer?
What is the secret to staying peaceful while busy?

4.21.summary: A person who does not scheme for things, who controls their mind and senses, who possesses nothing, and who acts only to maintain the body, commits no wrong even while acting.
questions: How can I act without constantly hoping for rewards?
How do I control my mind and senses in daily life?
Is it wrong to want things and plan for the future?
How can I live without being attached to possessions?
How do I act just to take care of my body without getting caught up in more?

4.22.summary: A person who is content with whatever comes without effort, who has gone beyond likes and dislikes, who is free from envy, and who stays even-minded in success and failure, remains unbound by karma even while acting.
questions: How can I be content with what I have instead of constantly striving for more?
How do I stop being jealous of others and comparing myself to them?
How can I stay calm whether I succeed or fail?
If I act without attachment, does that mean I won't be trapped by my actions?
What does it mean to go beyond pairs of opposites like pleasure and pain?

4.23.summary: A person who acts without attachment, whose mind is rooted in knowledge, and who works as an offering to the divine, is freed from the binding effects of their actions.
questions: How can I work without getting attached to the outcome?
What does it mean to offer my actions to God?
How do I become free from the consequences of my actions?
Can I be liberated while still doing my daily duties?

4.24.summary: This verse describes the ritual of sacrifice as a metaphor for action done with the awareness that everything involved—the offering, the ghee, the fire, and the one performing the sacrifice—is Brahman, and that such a person attains Brahman.
questions: How can I see the divine in everything I do?
What does it mean to act with awareness of Brahman?
How can ordinary actions become a form of worship?
How do I reach Brahman through my actions?
What is the significance of sacrifice in spiritual life?

4.25.summary: Some yogis perform rituals to gods, while others who have realized the Self offer the Self as a sacrifice in the fire of Brahman, meaning they dissolve their individual identity into the ultimate reality.
questions: What does it mean to offer the Self as a sacrifice?
How can I surrender my ego in daily life?
Are external rituals necessary for spiritual growth?
What is the fire of Brahman?
How do I know if I have realized the Self?

4.26.summary: Some yogis practice self-discipline by offering their senses, like hearing, into the fire of restraint, while others offer sense objects, like sound, into the fire of the senses.
questions: How can I control my senses when they keep pulling me toward distractions?
What does it mean to make my senses an offering rather than just suppressing them?
How do I deal with constantly wanting pleasurable experiences?
Are there different ways to practice self-discipline, and which one is right for me?
How can I turn everyday experiences into spiritual practice?

4.27.summary: This verse describes a form of spiritual sacrifice in which a person offers all the activities of their senses and their vital life force (breath) into the fire of self-control, a fire that is ignited by knowledge.
questions: How can I bring my senses and breath under control as a spiritual practice?
What does it mean to offer my actions and life energy into a fire of self-discipline?
How does knowledge help me master my senses and breath?
Can self-restraint be a form of worship?
What is the role of breath control in spiritual growth?

4.28.summary: This verse continues a list of different kinds of spiritual sacrifices, describing people who practice sacrifice by giving away wealth, by self-discipline, by yoga, and by studying scriptures, as well as those who follow very strict vows.
themes: wealth as a means of sacrifice
questions: I'm not sure what to do to feel closer to the divine—does this verse say there are many valid ways?
Can giving to others or doing my work with dedication be a form of spiritual practice?
Is studying and learning really a way to grow spiritually, or just something intellectual?
Do people who follow strict vows have an easier path, or is that just one option among many?

4.29.summary: This verse describes yogis who practice breath control (pranayama), offering the outgoing breath into the incoming and the incoming into the outgoing, as a form of sacrifice, completely absorbed in restraining the breath.
questions: I'm always anxious and can't calm my mind. How can controlling my breath help?
What does it mean to offer my breath as a sacrifice?
How can I use my breath to become more focused in daily life?
Is breath control a spiritual practice?
How do I practice pranayama as a form of yoga?

4.30.summary: Some practitioners control their eating and offer the breath forces within the breath forces; all such people understand sacrifice and have their sins destroyed by it.
questions: How can controlling what I eat become a spiritual practice?
What does it mean to offer my breath as a sacrifice?
How does sacrifice destroy my past mistakes?
Can simple disciplines like diet and breathing really lead to inner freedom?

4.31.summary: This verse teaches that those who perform sacrifices and consume the sacred remnants (prasada) attain the eternal Brahman, while those who neglect sacrifice fail to attain even this world, let alone the next.
themes: sacrifice as a path to liberation
questions: What happens to me if I don't fulfill my spiritual duties?
How can I experience grace in my daily life?
Why is it important to perform acts of sacrifice or service?
What does it mean to attain the eternal Brahman?
How does performing my duties affect my future well-being?

4.32.summary: Here Krishna explains that the many types of sacrifices described in the Vedas all arise from action, and that understanding this leads to liberation.
questions: What are the different kinds of sacrifices mentioned in the Vedas?
How can knowing that sacrifices come from action free me?
